claims.text: Nanoscale, compositionally distinct interfaces in multilayer high-entropy-alloy coatings increase resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation.
The interfaces impede dislocation glide and climb.
Interface obstruction of dislocations raises effective creep resistance at elevated temperatures.
The relevant interface-thickness range is from a few to dozens of nanometers.
Nanoindentation can characterize time-dependent deformation at small length scales in high-entropy alloys.
Coupling in-situ high-temperature nanoindentation with cross-sectional TEM can reveal real-time dislocation motion across multilayer interfaces.
Loads up to approximately 5 N are appropriate for the proposed indentation-creep comparison.
Dislocations accumulate at compositionally modulated interfaces and are obstructed there.
Dislocation accumulation at the interfaces produces local strain hardening and reduces creep rate.
Increased lattice misfit and interlayer chemical complexity aid the interface-mediated creep resistance.
Relative to a monolithic coating of the same nominal chemistry, the multilayer coating will have a lower steady-state creep rate.
Relative to the monolithic baseline, the multilayer coating will have a higher creep stress exponent.
Relative to the monolithic baseline, the multilayer coating will show less time-dependent indentation depth at elevated temperature.
Excessive layer thickness reduces dislocation blocking and makes creep resistance approach that of the monolithic baseline.
Insufficient compositional contrast reduces dislocation blocking and makes creep resistance approach that of the monolithic baseline.
Nanoindentation creep results may not extrapolate directly to bulk-component creep performance.
Small-scale tests already indicate interface-related strengthening in multilayer high-entropy-alloy coatings.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that insufficient compositional contrast should weaken interface blocking and move performance toward the baseline, whereas the falsification rule expects reduced compositional contrast to produce a decreased creep rate and increased stress exponent. These directional predictions are inconsistent.
